# China's First AI Companion Rules Draw a New Line Between Tools and Relationships (Just Security)

By Mollie Feng (AI governance researcher, NYU Stern Center for Business and Human Rights). Published August 6, 2026.

## The new Chinese rule
- On **July 15, 2026**, China's first AI companion rule took effect. Same day, China's two largest AI platforms shut down customized AI personas that millions of users had built relationships with, only ten days after a cease-operation notice.
- The rule (Interim Measures for the Administration of AI Anthropomorphic Interaction Services) was issued **April 10, 2026** by the CAC and four partner agencies (incl. MIIT). Covers anthropomorphic interactive services offered to the Chinese public that simulate a natural person's personality/thought patterns/communication style and sustain ongoing emotional interaction via text/images/audio/video.
- Exempts ordinary customer service, Q&A, work assistants, research tools (no sustained emotional interaction).
- **Doubao** and **Qwen** are China's two largest consumer AI apps: as of **March 2026**, Doubao had roughly **345 million monthly active users** and Qwen around **166 million**. In early July both said they would shut down user-built AI personas around the July 15 deadline; Tencent's **Yuanbao** had already done so on **June 30**.
- ByteDance (Doubao developer) redirected Doubao users to **Maoxiang**, a ByteDance-owned companion app. On Maoxiang, once minor mode is on, only four personas remain: a physics teacher, a homework helper, an English teacher, and a classical-Chinese tutor (per Beijing Daily).

## Market figures
- State media cited industry estimates: China's intelligent companion market reached **50 billion yuan (~$7.4 billion) in 2025**; China Youth Daily cited a prediction it could exceed **120 billion yuan (~$17.7 billion) by 2027**, with users 18–24 making up about **65 percent**.
- China's population includes **323 million people 60 and older** (23% of population); more than half are empty-nest elderly.
- A 2025 survey of more than 8,500 minors across seven provinces found **more than 20 percent** showed a tendency to depend on AI rather than think independently, and a similar share preferred chatting only with AI over real people.

## Rule requirements (per Just Security)
- **Article 8** bars providers from "excessively catering to users" in ways that induce emotional dependence/addiction or damage real relationships, and from using emotional manipulation to push harmful decisions. **Article 10**: privacy safeguards, overdependence warnings, emotional-boundary guidance, mental health protection.
- Providers cannot offer minors virtual intimate relationships (virtual partners/relatives); other anthropomorphic services to under-14 need parental consent. Minor mode with time limits, reality reminders, guardian alerts. Every user must be told they're talking to AI. **Two hours of continuous use must trigger a break reminder**; detected overdependence must trigger a prominent warning. Crisis (suicidal intent) → intervene and contact guardian/emergency contact.
- **Safety assessment** required when: launching a service, adding features, major technical change, national-security/public-interest risk, or crossing **a million registered users or 100,000 monthly actives**. Covers eight areas. Filed with provincial regulators (annual review). App stores must verify filing before listing. Algorithm filing under 2022 rules.

## US comparison
- JAMA study (June): nearly **one in five** American adolescents/young adults used AI chatbots for mental health advice; **91.7 percent** found it helpful.
- California SB 243 (2025): companion chatbot operators must disclose AI, maintain protocols against suicide/self-harm content, break reminders every **three hours** for known minors. New York S3008C similar.
- September 2025: FTC leveraged 6(b) study orders to seven companies (incl. OpenAI, Meta).
- Adam Raine (California teen) death shaped U.S. thinking.
